messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Conflict: Confrontations, Others Cycling: People cycling
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Kai presents as a 46-year-old software engineer, married, who reports escalating distress following an incident of police violence eight months prior. Before the event, Kai described themself as a person who valued order, logic, and a belief in civic structures. That foundation, they feel, has been entirely demolished. The traumatic event occurred during a peaceful daytime protest. Kai recalls the warmth of the sun and a feeling of profound, relaxed solidarity with the people around them. They were feeling hopeful, even happy. The shift was terrifyingly sudden. The police, who had been observing from a distance, advanced on bicycles. The memory from that point on loses all narrative cohesion. Kai cannot tell a clear story of what happened, even to themself. Instead, there are sensory fragments: the whirring sound of bicycle chains getting louder, a flash of a boot, the jarring impact of their shoulder against the pavement, and a wave of absolute terror and betrayal. When they try to force the memory into a linear sequence, their mind seems to shut down, pushing the fragments away before they can form a complete picture. More often, the experience returns not as an image but as pure emotion; sitting at their desk debugging code, Kai will suddenly be engulfed by the same sickening dread from that day, their heart pounding for a reason their conscious mind can't immediately place.

In the months since, Kai’s world has shrunk. The triggers are pervasive and often paradoxical. The most painful, they report, is the feeling of happiness itself. A quiet, relaxed evening with their spouse or a moment of satisfaction after solving a complex problem at work is inevitably followed by a surge of anxiety, a visceral certainty that feeling safe is a prelude to disaster. Confrontations of any kind, even a collegial debate about project strategy in a meeting, can trigger a powerful physical reaction. Kai describes their heart hammering against their ribs, sweat breaking out on their forehead, and an overwhelming urge to flee the room. They have started avoiding team meetings where technical disagreements are likely. This has been noticed by their manager, straining their professional standing. The most specific trigger is the sight and sound of people cycling. Living in the city, this is a daily occurrence. The simple sight of a cyclist coasting down the street or the click-and-whir of gears is enough to send a jolt of adrenaline through their system, forcing them to stop, brace themself, or change direction.

This constant sense of threat has reshaped Kai’s daily routines. At their open-plan tech office, they can no longer sit at their assigned desk in the middle of the floor. They arrive early each morning to claim a specific seat in the corner, back to the wall, where they can watch the entire room and no one can approach them from behind. They find themself constantly scanning colleagues and strangers on the subway, watching their hands and eyes for any sign of aggression or impending harm. They have come to believe that the world is a fundamentally unpredictable and hostile place, and you can never know who will harm you. This belief feels less like a thought and more like a fact. Accompanying this is a profound and painful sense of exposure. Kai is convinced that other people can see their trauma just by looking at them, that their fear is a visible stain on their skin. This makes eye contact feel unbearable and has led them to withdraw from friends, certain they are being judged for their perceived weakness.

The decision to seek therapy was prompted by their spouse. After Kai had a panic attack in response to their spouse’s suggestion of a relaxing weekend bike ride in the country, the couple had a difficult conversation. Kai acknowledged that their world had become a prison of their own making, and the constant vigilance was exhausting not only them but also the person they loved most. They came to therapy expressing a deep fear that they are permanently broken, that the person they were before the protest is gone forever. Their stated hope is simple, yet feels impossibly distant: to one day feel safe in their own body again.
